title: How social media feeds choose posts
examples: How does an algorithm know what I like?
What exactly is a filter bubble?
Can I escape a filter bubble?

explain.say: Today we are learning how social media feeds choose what you see. These feeds are not random at all. They use complex systems to decide the order of posts.

draw.text: How social media feeds choose posts
Feeds use algorithms to choose posts.

explain.say: The first key idea is the algorithm. This is basically a set of rules that decides what you see. It looks at what you and other users do online. For example, if you like dog pictures, the algorithm will show you more dog pictures.

Next we look at engagement. This means how much attention a post gets from people. High engagement signals to the algorithm that the post is interesting. For instance, a post with many comments gets boosted visibility.

The third concept is the filter bubble. This happens when the algorithm only shows you things it thinks you want to see. It can create a bubble of information around you. For example, if you only read about sports, you might never see news about science.

draw.text: Filter Bubble: Echo chamber of info.

explain.say: In real life, think about a radio station. If you only listen to one genre, the station might only play that music. This is like a filter bubble limiting your musical choices.

A common mistake is thinking the feed shows everything important. It really only shows what the algorithm predicts you will engage with. To avoid this, try looking at sources outside your usual topics.

faq.q: How does the algorithm know what I like?
faq.a: It tracks your past activity like what you stop scrolling on or what you share. It builds a profile based on these patterns.
asks: How do they track my interests?

faq.q: What is the difference between an algorithm and a filter bubble?
faq.a: The algorithm is the tool that sorts posts, and the filter bubble is the result when that tool only shows you similar things.
asks: Is a filter bubble caused by the algorithm?

faq.q: Can I really escape a filter bubble?
faq.a: It is difficult, but you can actively seek out information that challenges your current views. This helps break the pattern.
asks: How do I see different sides?
What can I do to broaden my view?

faq.q: Are algorithms always trying to trick me?
faq.a: They are designed to maximize your time on the platform, which can sometimes mean showing sensational content. It is a business goal.
asks: Are they designed to keep me hooked?

faq.a: No, engagement includes comments, shares, and how long you spend reading a post. All these actions count.

facts: Algorithms use complex rules to rank content visibility.
Engagement metrics include likes, shares, and comments.
A filter bubble limits exposure to diverse viewpoints.
Platforms use data from user behavior to refine feeds.

quiz.say: A user only sees posts about gaming and never sees posts about history. This is an example of:
quiz.why: The filter bubble describes the limited range of information you are shown.

wrong.1: The algorithm is the system doing the sorting, not the resulting limited view.
wrong.2: Engagement measures how much you interact, not what you are shown.
wrong.3: This is an action you take, not the limitation of your feed.

quiz.say: A post receives many shares and comments, making it appear higher up in the feed. This is mainly due to its:
quiz.why: High engagement signals tell the algorithm that the content is valuable to many people.

wrong.0: The algorithm uses engagement as one of many factors, but it is not the measure itself.
wrong.1: The filter bubble is the result of the feed, not the measure of a single post's popularity.
wrong.2: This is just one type of interaction; engagement covers many actions.
